locator.heading: Plums

source_text:
ARE so well known that they need no description.

_Government and virtues._] All Plums are under Venus, and are like
women, some better, and some worse. As there is great diversity of
kinds, so there is in the operation of Plums, for some that are sweet
moisten the stomach, and make the belly soluble; those that are sour
quench thirst more, and bind the belly; the moist and waterish do
sooner corrupt in the stomach, but the firm do nourish more, and offend
less. The dried fruit sold by the grocers under the names of Damask
Prunes, do somewhat loosen the belly, and being stewed, are often
used, both in health and sickness, to relish the mouth and stomach,
to procure appetite, and a little to open the body, allay choler, and
cool the stomach. Plum-tree leaves boiled in wine, are good to wash
and gargle the mouth and throat, to dry the flux of rheum coming to
the palate, gums, or almonds of the ear. The gum of the tree is good
to break the stone. The gum or leaves boiled in vinegar, and applied,
kills tetters and ringworms. Matthiolus saith, The oil preserved out of
the kernels of the stones, as oil of almonds is made, is good against
the inflamed piles, the tumours or swellings of ulcers, hoarseness of
the voice, roughness of the tongue and throat, and likewise the pains
in the ears. And that five ounces of the said oil taken with one ounce
of muskadel, drives forth the stone, and helps the cholic.

pubmed.title: Plum Pit Bezoar.
pubmed.relevance_note: Discusses traditional use of plum pits for digestive issues and bezoars, aligning with 'stone' and 'belly looseness' uses.

pubmed.title: Dried Plums, Prunes and Bone Health: A Comprehensive Review.
pubmed.relevance_note: Reviews modern nutritional benefits of prunes, potentially addressing 'appetite' and general digestive health.

pubmed.title: Traditional wound-healing plants used in the Balkan region (Southeast Europe).
pubmed.relevance_note: Documents traditional applications of Prunus species for skin conditions like ringworms and wound healing in the Balkans.

evidence.summary: Evidence supports traditional uses of P. domestica parts (pits, fruit) for digestive regulation ('belly looseness', 'stone') and skin conditions ('ringworms'). Modern reviews highlight nutritional value for appetite and bone health, while ethnobotanical studies confirm wound-healing applications in Southeast Europe.

concordance.rationale: Modern evidence (PMID: 28422064) supports bone health but lacks clinical data for thirst, appetite, or skin conditions. No EMA approval exists.
concordance.uncertainty: High due to absence of direct clinical trials for historical indications like choler or stones in modern literature.
caveats: Historical 'choler' is not a modern medical condition.
Safety concerns exist regarding pit toxicity (PMID: 35065750).

issues: Unearned Grade: The entry received a 'C' grade with 'partial' direction based on modern evidence (PMID: 28422064) for bone health. However, the historical indications (thirst, appetite, skin conditions, choler, stones) have zero EMA approval and no direct clinical trial support in modern literature. The presence of a failed quote regarding traditional 'sweet/moisten' properties without corresponding modern validation or safety confirmation (given pit toxicity concerns) makes the grade unjustified for the full scope of historical claims.

Completeness Gap: The selected taxon 'Prunus domestica' lacks family resolution in the candidates list, and the 'Damask Prunes' entry remains ambiguous with no scientific name selected despite high confidence in one candidate.

Safety Warning Ignored: The rationale explicitly cites safety concerns regarding pit toxicity (PMID: 35065750), yet the entry does not flag this as a critical limitation or contraindication for the historical uses involving consumption of pits or seeds.
